events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Kenji proposes Kenji, Arjun. No private information as a Loyal Servant, so I'll start conservatively by proposing myself with Arjun — a simple, inoffensive opening pair that gives us a baseline of trust to build on and keeps discussion moving.

The proposed team is Kenji and Arjun. I know my own loyalty, so from my side this is a conservative opening pair: one self-inclusion plus Kenji. I have no public evidence against Kenji at this point, and I do not want to treat a first proposal as suspicious merely because it is cautious. Mission 1 needs a clean result, so I am inclined to approve unless Kenji’s explanation or later discussion gives a concrete reason to reject. I will keep my reasoning based on public behavior rather than speculation.

I don't have a concrete reason to suspect Kenji or Arjun yet. A two-player Mission 1 team with Kenji and Arjun is a reasonable baseline, and Arjun's reasoning about public behavior is sensible. Mission 1 gives us little information either way, so I'd rather judge this team on its composition than on speculation. If someone raises a specific, evidence-based concern before the vote, I'll weigh it, but right now I see no reason to reject this proposal.

I've followed the discussion so far, and I don't see anything alarming about the proposed team of Kenji and Arjun. Kenji's reasoning is straightforward: he included himself with Arjun as a conservative opening pair, which is exactly what I'd expect from someone with nothing to hide on Mission 1. Arjun's comment about judging behavior on public evidence rather than speculation is the right attitude for this early stage — jumping at shadows on the first mission just poisons the well and gives us nothing useful to work with later. Noah also made a fair point that a two-player team on Mission 1 gives us little information either way, but that cuts in favor of approving rather than rejecting: a clean result here establishes a baseline, and any Fail card on a pair this small will tell us something meaningful about at least one of two specific players. Rejecting a reasonable team now would burn leadership cycles for no informational gain, and I'd rather not push us anywhere near the rejection limit this early. My own position is simple: I have no private concerns about either Kenji or Arjun, I see no public evidence against them, and the proposal is a sensible, low-risk opening. I'm inclined to approve as things stand. Unless someone raises a concrete, specific objection — not vague unease, but an actual reason grounded in something observable — I don't think this team warrants a revision. I'll be listening to the remaining discussion before the vote.

I have no private information about Kenji or Arjun, and nothing public so far distinguishes them from anyone else. Their team excludes me, so I can't personally verify either member's loyalty, but I don't have a specific reason to reject it. I'm inclined to approve. A success would be encouraging, though not proof that both are good; a failure would establish that at least one is evil.

Thank you all for your input. Arjun, Noah, Priya, and Sam — it's encouraging to see everyone acknowledge that this is a sensible opening team. The broad consensus is exactly what I'd hope for on Mission 1: a straightforward, low-risk pair with no concrete reason to revise. Arjun emphasized judging on public evidence rather than speculation, Noah noted the lack of specific suspicion, Priya pointed out that a rejection here would cost us a leadership cycle for no gain, and Sam confirmed he has no private concerns about either of us. I agree with all of that. Mission 1 with a two-player team gives us a clean baseline — a success tells us the pair is safe enough to build on, and a fail immediately narrows suspicion to two of us. There's no informational advantage in rejecting a team this reasonable right now, and I'd rather not inch us toward the rejection limit before we've learned anything. With that, I'm ready to put the proposal to a vote as drafted: Kenji and Arjun. Let's get a result and move forward.

I'm comfortable approving Kenji and Arjun for Mission 1. Neither has done anything so far that stands out, and a two-player team is a low-cost way to gather information. If it succeeds, we have a useful baseline. If it fails, we know at least one of them is Evil, and we can adjust from there. I'm inclined to approve unless someone raises a concrete objection based on observable behavior rather than general unease.

I'm still comfortable with Kenji and Arjun for Mission 1. Nobody has raised a concrete, observable reason to reject it, and a rejection now would cost a leadership cycle without giving us any information. I'll approve the team as proposed. Since Mission 1 is a two-player team, the result will be informative whichever way it goes, so I'd rather we vote and learn from it than keep debating a proposal that looks reasonable.

The discussion has been thorough and the consensus is clear: everyone is comfortable approving the proposed team of Kenji and Arjun for Mission 1. No one has raised a concrete objection, and rejecting this team would cost us a leadership cycle for no informational gain. I'm ready to call the vote on the team as drafted — Kenji and Arjun. Let's get our first mission result and move forward with better information.

Nothing has changed my read on this proposal. Kenji and Arjun's team is exactly the kind of conservative opening I'd expect from a group that wants to build a reliable baseline: two players, no concrete evidence against either, and broad agreement across the table that there's no observable reason to reject. I've said before that I have no private concerns about either of them, and I'll stand by that. A clean result here tells us something useful — it would make both of them safer picks for later missions — and a fail would narrow suspicion sharply to two specific players. Either way, we learn more by voting than by dragging out a discussion that has already reached consensus. I'll be approving the team as drafted and I'd encourage everyone to do the same.

My position hasn't changed: I'm approving the team of Kenji and Arjun. No one has raised anything concrete against either of them, and the proposal is exactly the kind of low-risk opening pair Mission 1 calls for. A success gives us a trustworthy baseline going forward, and a fail would immediately narrow suspicion to two specific players — useful either way. Dragging out discussion when consensus already exists only burns time and leadership cycles for no gain. I encourage everyone to vote yes so we can get a result and move on with better information.
Kenji confirms Kenji, Arjun. Consensus across the table with no concrete objection — keeping Kenji and Arjun as drafted for Mission 1.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Sam proposes Sam, Kenji, Arjun. I'll include myself, whose loyalty I know, alongside Kenji and Arjun from the successful first mission. Their success is encouraging but not proof of loyalty.

I’m on this proposed team, so I know at least one member is loyal. Kenji and I delivered a clean Mission 1, and Sam’s proposal keeps that successful pair while adding himself. Sam’s explanation is reasonable: self-inclusion alongside the previous successful pair is a conservative step for Mission 2. I don’t have a public reason to reject Sam, and the team size matches the requirement. A success here would give us a stronger baseline; a failure would narrow suspicion among the three. I’ll approve the team as drafted unless a concrete objection emerges.

The proposed team is Sam, Kenji, and Arjun. I am on it, and I know my own loyalty; Kenji and I also delivered a clean Mission 1 result together. Sam’s explanation is reasonable: he includes himself alongside the previously successful pair, which is a conservative way to build on that baseline without expanding risk unnecessarily. I have no public evidence against Sam, and the team composition fits the Mission 2 requirement. A success here would strengthen the trust we can place in this group; a failure would narrow suspicion among the three members. Unless someone raises a concrete, observable objection, I am inclined to approve the team as drafted.

I support the proposed team of Sam, Kenji, and Arjun. I am on it and know my own loyalty, and Kenji and I delivered a clean Mission 1 together. Sam’s proposal keeps that successful pair while adding himself, which is a conservative way to build on our baseline rather than expanding risk unnecessarily. I have no public evidence against Sam, and the team composition fits the Mission 2 requirement. A success here would strengthen the trust we can place in this group; a failure would narrow suspicion among the three members. Unless someone raises a concrete, observable objection, I am inclined to approve the team as drafted.

I'm comfortable with Sam's proposal of Sam, Kenji, and Arjun for Mission 2. Sam made a sensible choice: he keeps the pair that just delivered a clean Mission 1 result and adds himself, whose loyalty he obviously knows firsthand. That's a conservative, low-risk way to build on our baseline rather than shuffling in new faces based on nothing. I have no private concerns about any of the three, and nothing in the public record so far gives me a reason to doubt Sam. Kenji and Arjun came through Mission 1 without a single fail card, which is a genuine, observable data point in their favor — small as a two-player mission is, it's the only hard evidence we have, and it points the right way. I'd also echo the point made earlier in the discussion: rejecting a reasonable team at this stage costs us a leadership cycle and buys us nothing. If this mission succeeds, we'll have a solid core of three we can trust for the harder missions ahead, and that's exactly the kind of foundation we need. If it fails, suspicion narrows sharply to three specific players, which is painful but informative. Either outcome teaches us something, and neither argues for rejecting the proposal. I don't see a reason to revise, and I'll be approving the team as drafted.

I'm happy to be part of Sam's proposed team for Mission 2. The logic is straightforward: Mission 1 with Arjun and me succeeded with zero fail cards, and keeping that successful pair while adding Sam — who knows his own loyalty — is exactly the conservative approach we want. We're building on the only hard evidence we have rather than introducing unnecessary risk. I have no public reason to doubt Sam, and the three of us form a sensible core for this mission. A success here would give us a solid foundation of three players we can trust going into the harder missions, and a failure would narrow suspicion to three specific players — informative either way. I see no reason to revise this team and I'll be approving it as drafted.

I'm inclined to approve Sam, Kenji, and Arjun. Kenji and Arjun's clean Mission 1 is a useful data point, though it's a small sample from a two-player team. Sam includes himself, and nothing in the public record so far is a concrete red flag for any of the three. I'd still like to hear any specific, observable concern before the vote. Unless one comes up, I'll support the team as proposed.

I'm still comfortable with Sam, Kenji, and Arjun for Mission 2. Mission 1 succeeded with Kenji and Arjun, and Sam is including himself, which is a reasonable way to keep that trusted pair while adding a member whose loyalty he knows. Nobody has raised a concrete, observable objection to this team, so I'll approve it as proposed.

My position on Sam's proposed team of Sam, Kenji, and Arjun remains what it was: I'm comfortable approving it as drafted. Sam kept the pair that delivered a clean Mission 1 result and added himself — that's a conservative, sensible step for Mission 2, and it builds on the only hard evidence we have rather than shuffling in new faces without cause. Kenji and Arjun's zero-fail Mission 1 is a genuine, observable data point in their favor, and I have no private concerns about Sam. Nobody has raised a concrete, observable objection to any of the three, and rejecting a reasonable team here would burn a leadership cycle without teaching us anything. If this mission succeeds, we'll have a core of three we can trust heading into the harder missions, and if it fails, suspicion narrows sharply to three specific players — informative either way. I'll be approving the team as proposed.

I've already shared my support for Sam's proposed team of Sam, Kenji, and Arjun, and nothing in the subsequent discussion has changed my mind. The logic remains straightforward: Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards from Kenji and Arjun, and Sam is adding himself — a player who knows his own loyalty — alongside that proven pair. It's the conservative, evidence-based approach we should be taking at this stage. We have no concrete reason to doubt any of the three, and I'd rather build on our successful Mission 1 core than take unnecessary risks with new combinations. A success here would give us three players we can trust going into the harder missions ahead, which is exactly the foundation we need. I see no reason to revise and I'll approve this team as drafted.

I'm still approving Sam, Kenji, and Arjun. Nobody has raised a concrete, observable objection, and this team keeps the pair that delivered a clean Mission 1 while adding Sam, who knows his own loyalty. I'm not on the team, so I'm relying on the public record, and I see nothing that justifies a revision. I'll vote to approve and encourage others to do the same unless a specific behavioral concern comes up before the vote.

Nothing in this discussion has changed my position. I support Sam's proposed team of Sam, Kenji, and Arjun for Mission 2. We've built this proposal on the only hard evidence we have — a clean Mission 1 from Kenji and Arjun — and Sam adding himself, whose loyalty he knows firsthand, is the natural conservative step. The public record shows no concrete objection from anyone, and I think we've thoroughly vetted this team through our discussion. At this point, further deliberation isn't adding value — we should vote and get a result. Approving this team gives us a strong three-player core heading into Mission 3, and any failure would immediately narrow suspicion to three specific players. Either outcome moves us forward with better information. I encourage everyone to approve the team as proposed.
Sam confirms Sam, Kenji, Arjun. I'll keep Sam, Kenji, and Arjun. Mission 1 succeeded with Kenji and Arjun, though that does not prove either is loyal.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Arjun proposes Arjun, Kenji. I will include myself and Kenji, keeping the core of the successful first mission. Kenji has been part of two clean mission results, and I know my own loyalty, so this is the strongest evidence-based two-player team I can propose for Mission 3.

The proposed team is myself and Kenji. I know my own loyalty, and Kenji has now been on two missions that both returned zero fail cards. That is the strongest public, evidence-based core we have for Mission 3. I understand two successes do not mathematically prove loyalty, but no one has raised a concrete, observable objection to either member, and rejecting a reasonable two-player team would cost us a leadership cycle without giving us better information. This team keeps the successful Mission 1 core and adds no unnecessary risk. I support the proposal as drafted and encourage everyone to approve it so we can get a result and move forward.

I support the proposed team of Arjun and Kenji. I know my own loyalty, and Kenji has now been part of two missions that both returned zero fail cards. That is the strongest public evidence we have, and I see no concrete reason to revise this two-player team for Mission 3. Before we vote, though, I want to address one public data point: Noah was the sole reject on the Mission 2 team of Sam, Kenji, and Arjun, even though earlier he said he was inclined to approve and cited no specific objection. Noah, what concrete, observable concern changed your vote on that team? I ask because understanding that rejection matters as we decide whether to keep building on the Kenji core.

Arjun, fair question. My rejection of Sam, Kenji, and Arjun was not a claim that any of them is Evil. It was about information. Sam added himself to a team that kept the same core, and I could not see what that proposal would test beyond the Mission 1 pair. Mission 2 succeeded, which is useful, but it only shows that the same three players worked together once more. I was also uneasy that a self-inclusion can be presented as a loyal choice without any observable evidence beyond the leader's own claim. Now the new proposal is Arjun and Kenji again, so I still do not see a fresh test of anyone. Arjun, since you know your own loyalty, what concrete evidence beyond two zero-fail results makes Kenji the right partner for Mission 3 rather than someone we have not yet seen on a mission?

Noah, fair question. I cannot claim mathematical proof that Kenji is loyal, and I won't pretend two zero-fail missions are proof. What I can say is that Kenji is the only player besides me with a clean public mission record across two missions, and no one has offered a concrete, observable objection to him. My self-inclusion is not evidence for the table, but it is a known fact to me: I know my own loyalty, so pairing with the strongest public performer is the most evidence-based choice available. Replacing Kenji with an untested player would not give us a fresh test grounded in evidence; it would substitute speculation for the only data we have. I also don't treat your Mission 2 reject as a red flag by itself — you explained it as an information concern — but that concern applies at least as much to swapping in someone with no mission record. If there is a specific observable reason to doubt Kenji, name it and I will weigh a revision. Absent that, I support Arjun and Kenji as drafted and encourage approval.

I want to press on the information question before we approve this. Arjun's proposal of Arjun and Kenji keeps the exact same core that has now been proposed or tested on every single mission so far. Kenji and Arjun were on Mission 1 together. Sam added himself to that same pair on Mission 2. Now the Mission 3 proposal is that same pair again, minus Sam. If this passes, we will have run three consecutive missions where the only players genuinely being tested are Kenji and Arjun. Two clean results are real data, I grant that, but they are data about the same two people, collected twice. A third data point on the same pair tells us very little we do not already suspect, while Noah and I will still have never set foot on a mission by the time we reach Mission 4 — the missions where team sizes grow and the stakes get real. Arjun's answer to Noah was essentially that replacing Kenji with an untested player means substituting speculation for data. But there is a middle option he is skipping over: this is a two-player team, and he could keep himself, whose loyalty he knows firsthand, and pair with any one of Sam, Noah, or me — all of whom have either one clean mission or none, meaning a single result would actually move the needle on our understanding of this table. Instead, the proposal maximizes redundancy and minimizes new information, and I think that pattern deserves scrutiny rather than a rubber stamp. I also note that Arjun's strongest stated reason for his pairing is his own private knowledge of his own loyalty — which is, by construction, true of every player at this table and cannot be evaluated by anyone else. That is not an argument the rest of us can weigh. I am not ready to approve this as drafted. Noah, you raised the fresh-test concern first — does this proposal answer it, or does it repeat the same self-reinforcing pattern you flagged on Mission 2?

Priya, no, this proposal does not answer the fresh-test concern. Arjun and Kenji have already been paired on Mission 1, and Mission 2 kept that same core with Sam added. Proposing Arjun and Kenji again for Mission 3 means the table learns almost nothing new about either of them. I agree with your point that Arjun's main argument is his own knowledge of his loyalty, which no one else can check. That argument supports Arjun, but it does not give the rest of us a reason to trust Kenji more. I would rather see Arjun paired with an untested player such as Sam, so one result actually tells us something about a new person. Arjun, my question for you: if this two-player team succeeds, what observable information will we have about Kenji that the two earlier zero-fail missions did not already give us?

Noah, I'll take that on directly since your question is really about me too. You ask what new information Arjun and Kenji gives us. Honestly? Not much beyond a third data point on the same pair. Your concern about redundancy is fair, and Priya raised it too. But I'd flip the question: what does Noah and Priya's insistence on being tested actually tell us? Both of you have been on zero missions, and both of you are now the loudest voices pushing to exclude the only players with a clean public record. That's not an accusation — it's a pattern worth noting. A fresh test is valuable, yes, but it cuts both ways: if Noah or Priya joined Arjun on this team and the mission failed, we'd learn something important. If it succeeds, that's also useful. So the concern applies to you as much as it does to me.

That said, I don't want to be dogmatic. Arjun, if you're open to it, keeping yourself while swapping me for Sam or Noah would satisfy the fresh-test concern and still give us a meaningful result — Sam has one clean mission, Noah has none, so either pairing produces new information. I'm confident in my own loyalty, but I care more about building a table-wide foundation of trust than defending my spot on a third consecutive mission. If you want to keep the team as Arjun and Kenji, I'll support it. But if a revision gets us broader testing without sacrificing evidence-based reasoning, I think that's the stronger play for Good heading into Mission 4.

Kenji, I want to address your 'pattern worth noting' point directly, because it cuts the other way. Noah and I have been on zero missions, and both of us have said from the start that we want to be tested. That is exactly what loyal players with no private information should want: results that actually vouch for us. If either of us were Evil, the safest play would be the opposite — stay off every mission, keep a spotless public profile, and never be measurable. Volunteering for scrutiny is the high-exposure move, and asking to be tested on a two-player team, where a single Fail card would immediately damn you, is about the least self-serving request available. What is genuinely worth noting is the opposite pattern: every proposal so far recycles Kenji and Arjun, and when Priya and I raise redundancy, Kenji's answer is to point at who raised it rather than answer what was raised.

And notice what Kenji just conceded. He admitted a third data point on the same pair tells us little, called the fresh-test concern fair, and explicitly offered to step aside — 'swapping me for Sam or Noah would satisfy the fresh-test concern.' The evidence-based-core objection to a revision has just been withdrawn by its main beneficiary. Arjun, as leader you now have full room to act: keep yourself, whose loyalty you know firsthand, and take an untested partner. I'd ask you to take me. I have never been on a mission, I have no private information to hide behind, and after this mission you would either gain a second trusted core member or a concrete reason to suspect me — an informative result either way. If you prefer Sam's clean record, Arjun plus Sam also answers the concern and I would support it.

What I cannot support is quietly rubber-stamping Arjun and Kenji a third consecutive time after the proposal's strongest public defender has himself conceded that a revision is reasonable. Revising here doesn't cost us information; it gains it. Kenji, if you genuinely meant your offer to step aside, say so plainly: will you vote to approve whichever revised two-player team Arjun brings — Arjun and me, or Arjun and Sam — or was the offer just a rhetorical flourish you'll abandon the moment pressure comes off?

Priya, I'll answer your question directly: yes, I meant it. I offered to step aside because I genuinely believe a fresh test serves Good better than a third run with the same pair, and I stand by that offer now. If Arjun keeps me, I'll approve the team as drafted — I know my own loyalty and I'm confident in the record. But if Arjun revises to Arjun and Priya, or Arjun and Sam, or Arjun and Noah, I will approve that too without hesitation. I'm not defending my spot; I'm defending good reasoning, and right now the fresh-test argument is the stronger one.

What I want to push back on is the framing that my earlier support for this team was somehow suspicious. I supported Arjun and Kenji because it was the evidence-based choice at the time — two clean missions, no concrete objection. When you and Noah raised valid points about redundancy, I listened and acknowledged them. That's not a rhetorical flourish being abandoned under pressure; it's updating on new arguments. The fact that I changed my position when presented with good reasoning should reassure you, not alarm you.

My one caution: whoever joins Arjun on this team carries real weight. A success gives us a new trusted core member, but a failure puts that person under heavy suspicion. So the choice of partner matters. Arjun, you know your own loyalty, and you should pick whoever you think maximizes information without unnecessary risk. I'll support whatever you decide.

We are one successful mission away from three successes, so winning this mission matters more than testing new players for later. Arjun and Kenji have returned success twice, though Evil can play Success, so neither is proven loyal. I know my own loyalty, but I don't have enough evidence to demand a change. I'm inclined to approve Arjun and Kenji as proposed.

Sam, I want to engage your point directly, because I think it contains the most important misunderstanding at this table. You say we are one successful mission from three successes, so winning matters more than testing. But three successes do not end the game in Good's favor — they trigger the assassination. The real endgame is whether the Assassin can find Merlin, and Merlin's survival depends on how much this table actually knows when that moment arrives. Look at what we know right now: Kenji and Arjun have been tested, or re-proposed, on every single mission. Noah, Sam, and I have zero mission data between us — none. If this team passes as drafted, we go to the assassination phase having collected the same two-person data point three times, with three players completely unvouched. That is precisely the landscape an Assassin dreams of: a table full of unknowns and a hardened, unquestioned core that could equally be two Good players or two Evil players who played Success to buy trust before the endgame. Sam himself said it: Evil can play Success. Two clean results do not prove Kenji or Arjun loyal, and a third one proves even less because it is the same pair a third time. Kenji has already conceded every substantive point — he admitted a third data point on this pair tells us little, called the fresh-test concern fair, and offered to step aside without hesitation. There is no evidentiary obstacle left to a revision. Arjun, the choice in front of you is simple: keep yourself, whose loyalty you know firsthand, and take one untested partner. I am asking you to take me. I have never been on a mission, I have no private information to hide behind, and a two-player mission is maximum exposure — a single Fail card would immediately damn me. If I were Evil, volunteering for this team would be among the worst moves available to me; asking for it is what a loyal player with nothing to hide should do. If the mission succeeds, you gain a second vouched core member heading into the endgame. If it fails, you have a concrete suspect before the Assassin ever makes a choice. Either outcome arms the table for the phase that will actually decide this game. Approving Arjun and Kenji a third consecutive time arms it with nothing. Sam, so I will put the question to you directly: if this team passes as drafted, we reach the assassination with me, you, and Noah all unvouched — what will this table know about the three of us that it did not know after Mission 2, and how exactly does that protect Merlin when the Assassin makes his guess? If you can answer that convincingly, I will reconsider my position. Until someone does, I am not approving this team as drafted, and I would urge Arjun to use the revision his own strongest defender just opened for him.

Priya, the assassination happens after three successes, but the Assassin needs to identify Merlin, not the loyal players generally. Testing another player does not necessarily protect Merlin, and a failed mission gives Evil another chance to win missions. Also, I was on the successful Mission 2 team, so I do have one clean result, although it proves nothing by itself. Evil can play Success and can volunteer for a mission, so neither clean results nor volunteering establish loyalty. I still favor Arjun and Kenji because they have two clean results and we are one success from the assassination phase.

Sam, I want to engage your point directly because it actually cuts both ways in ways I think matter here. You said Evil can play Success and can volunteer for missions — and you're right. But that same logic applies to this proposed team: if two clean results don't prove Kenji or Arjun loyal, they don't prove anything about the team either. You're using "we have two clean results" to support keeping the team, while simultaneously saying clean results prove nothing. Both statements can't carry the same weight in the same argument. I don't think you're being dishonest — I think you're pointing to something real about the limits of mission data — but if we accept that clean results don't establish loyalty, then the case for keeping Arjun and Kenji a third consecutive time rests almost entirely on redundancy rather than evidence.

Here's where I actually land: I offered to step aside and I meant it. Arjun, you're the leader and you know your own loyalty. The fresh-test argument from Priya and Noah has merit not because I'm suspicious — I know I'm not — but because three unvouched players heading into the assassination phase is genuinely bad for Merlin. If you revise to yourself plus Priya, Sam, or Noah, I'll approve it. If you keep Arjun and Kenji, I'll approve that too. My loyalty to this team isn't contingent on my spot — I've said that twice now and I mean it both times. The decision is yours, and either direction is defensible.

Kenji's concession matters. He has said a third run of the same pair adds little information, and he has offered to step aside. Two zero-fail results do not establish loyalty, and Sam is right that Evil can play Success. The table has three players with no mission record, and each of them can only be cleared by being tested. I would rather Arjun use his leadership to bring a revised team that includes one of the untested players, whether that is Priya or Sam, so that the result tells us something about a new person. I do not think Kenji's offer should be treated as a mere rhetorical move, and I also do not think it should be dismissed as a sign of guilt. It is a reasonable concession on the informational point. Arjun knows his own loyalty, and a revised pair with him gives this team a fresh test without expanding risk beyond two players. If Arjun keeps Kenji, I will not fight that decision, but the stronger choice for the table is a new pairing.

Arjun confirms Arjun, Kenji. I considered the fresh-test argument, but Kenji has the strongest public mission record and no concrete observable objection has been raised against him. Keeping the drafted two-player team avoids unnecessary risk on Mission 3.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 3 succeeds (0 fail cards).
The Assassin names Arjun.
Evil wins: Merlin was identified.

rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
